statutorySection: Ind AS 36 (Impairment of Assets) converged with IAS 36 and aligned with US GAAP ASC 360/350
title: Impairment of Assets & Cash-Generating Units (Recoverable Amount Determination, Goodwill Priority Allocation, and Reversal Boundaries)

effectivePeriod.annualReset: Annual mandatory impairment test for goodwill and intangible assets with indefinite useful lives; indicator-based testing for other assets
effectivePeriod.sunsetNotes: Mandatory standard notified via MCA G.S.R. 111(E) effective FY 2015-16 onwards.

plainTextSummary: Under Ind AS 36 (converged with IAS 36 and aligned with US GAAP ASC 360 & 350), an entity ensures that its assets are carried at no more than their recoverable amount. An asset is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount. The recoverable amount of an asset or a cash-generating unit (CGU) is the higher of: (1) its fair value less costs of disposal (the price that would be received to sell an asset in an orderly transaction between market participants less incremental direct costs); and (2) its value in use (the present value of the future cash flows expected to be derived from an asset or CGU using a pre-tax discount rate reflecting current market assessments of the time value of money and risks specific to the asset). If the recoverable amount is less than the carrying amount, the carrying amount of the asset or CGU is reduced to its recoverable amount and the difference is recognized immediately as an impairment loss in Profit and Loss. For a CGU, the impairment loss is allocated first to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill allocated to the unit, and then pro-rata to the other assets of the unit based on their relative carrying amounts (subject to asset floor constraints where no asset is reduced below the highest of fair value less costs of disposal, value in use, or zero). Goodwill impairment cannot be reversed under any circumstances; impairment losses for other assets are assessed annually and reversed if estimates have changed, capped at depreciated historical cost.
